title: Scheduler lockup + eviction mitigation playbook
content:
Summary:
This is a runbook-style playbook for incidents where the kube-scheduler appears to stop making scheduling decisions (lockup/hang) and we observe a downstream spike in pod evictions and pods stuck Pending. In the last incident (2024-11-06) a combo of ephemeral leader election delay + scheduler goroutine stall coincided with a CNI reconnection flurry and caused ~120 pods to be evicted over ~7 minutes, with customer-facing latency spikes for low-latency services.

Why this doc exists:
- On-call often assumes node pressure or CNI is primary; when scheduler is unhealthy the right remediation is to restore scheduler progress and avoid mass evictions which make recovery worse.
- Provide detection signals, triage commands, immediate mitigations, and long-term fixes.

Impact profile (typical):
- Pods stuck in Pending for scheduling, controller-manager backlog.
- Eviction spikes as nodes briefly report pressure or Pods exceed disruption budget.
- Increased API server writes and watch churn.
- Customer API latency and some 5xxs from restarted pods.

Detection (metrics & alerts):
- Alert: scheduler_schedules_per_second drops below 0.1 or near-zero for >30s.
- Alert: Increase in kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total per-cluster above baseline.
- Alert: sudden rise in kube_node_status_condition{condition="Ready",status="false"} across multiple nodes (could be CNI flaps).
- Grafana dashboards to check: Scheduling latency, scheduling throughput, apiserver request rates, kube-scheduler pod CPU/mem and thread stacks.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Verify symptoms:
   - kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l component=kube-scheduler -o wide
   - kubectl top pod -n kube-system <scheduler-pod> (or check node if static pod)
   - kubectl get events --all-namespaces --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 200
2) Check scheduler logs for stalls, panic, or leader election churn:
   - kubectl logs -n kube-system <scheduler-pod> --since=15m | grep -E "error|panic|failed|leader|stalled|deadlock" -i
   - If static pod on control-plane node: ssh to control plane and inspect /var/log/pods or container runtime logs.
3) Confirm if APIServer or etcd latencies are contributing:
   - kubectl get --raw '/metrics' | grep apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket
   - Check etcd leader changes / etcd_server_has_leader metric.
4) Check CNI/node readiness (to rule out false positives):
   - kubectl get nodes -o wide
   - kubectl describe node <node-name> | egrep "Network|kubelet|eviction|Allocatable|OutOf" -A3
   - Check CNI pod logs (e.g., calico/node, amazon-vpc-cni) in kube-system namespace.

Immediate remediation steps (ordered):
A) If scheduler pods are unhealthy or logs show deadlock/stall:
   - If using Deployment/DaemonSet: kubectl rollout restart deployment kube-scheduler -n kube-system
   - If static pod: ssh to control plane node and restart kubelet/systemd unit for the static manifest (sudo systemctl restart kubelet) or rotate static pod manifest (move then restore)
   - After restart: confirm scheduling resumes: kubectl get --raw '/metrics' | grep scheduler_schedules_per_second
B) Avoid mass automated evictions while repairing:
   - If eviction controller is too aggressive, temporarily raise eviction thresholds on affected nodes via kubelet flags (only if safe): --eviction-hard temporarily increased to allow breathing room (coordination with SRE lead required).
   - Alternatively, cordon most-affected nodes to stop new pods scheduling to unstable nodes: kubectl cordon <node>
   - Use kubectl drain with --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data for safe evictions if you must migrate pods, but prefer to restore scheduler and allow controllers to reconcile.
C) If CNI flaps coincide (packets/liveness probes failing):
   - Restart CNI DaemonSet pods one-at-a-time on problem nodes: kubectl rollout restart ds <cni-ds> -n kube-system
   - Check kernel conntrack table pressure (ss -s or /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count) on node. If near limit, coordinate node-level conntrack tuning.

Commands cheat-sheet (copyable):
- kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l component=kube-scheduler -o wide
- kubectl logs -n kube-system <scheduler-pod> --tail=200
- kubectl get --raw '/metrics' | grep scheduler_schedules_per_second
- kubectl get nodes -o wide; kubectl describe node <node>
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force (use with caution)
- kubectl rollout restart deployment kube-scheduler -n kube-system

When to escalate:
- Scheduler restart does not restore schedules within 2 minutes.
- etcd leader changes repeatedly or etcd write latency > 1s.
- More than 20 nodes show NotReady within 5 minutes.
- Business-impacting customer errors (SLO breach).
Escalation path: page SRE on-call -> oncall lead -> infra-engineering -> applied-ml infra owner if customer models affected.

Post-incident actions and diagnosis: 
- Collect scheduler goroutine stacks (kubectl exec to get pprof if enabled or grep logs) + apiserver traces.
- Correlate scheduler_schedules_per_second with apiserver request latency and etcd metrics to find root cause ordering.
- If CNI flapping contributed, capture CNI pod logs and node-level kernel messages (dmesg) for possible kernel/network driver issues.
- If conntrack pressure observed, file infra ticket to increase table size and add monitoring alert.

Longer-term fixes / action items (owners added):
1) Add a synthetic scheduling probe and a specific alert for scheduler stagnation (PR: #87) - Owner: Marcus Chen - ETA: 2 weeks.
2) Harden leader election config and reduce leader lock TTL to shorten failover detection for scheduler - Owner: Priya Nair - ETA: 4 weeks.
3) Improve runbook automation: auto-restart kube-scheduler if schedules/sec is zero for 45s (with exponential backoff and circuit breaker) - Owner: SRE Tools - ETA: 6 weeks.
4) Run a chaos test for CNI restart under load to validate behavior and eviction rate - Owner: Platform Eng - ETA: 3 weeks.
5) Add conntrack pressure alert and automated node cordon if kernel table exceeds 80% - Owner: Infra Eng - ETA: 3 weeks.

Notes / gotchas from last incident:
- Restarting all scheduler replicas at once caused a brief double-schedule churn; prefer one at a time if using multiple replicas.
- On static-pod control planes, kubelet restarts can surface unrelated systemd services flapping; coordinate with platform eng before restart during business hours.
- Eviction controller and HPA can interact in surprising ways; check HPA scale-down policies before mass drain.

Appendix: quick evidence checklist to attach to postmortem:
- Scheduler logs (time window)
- APIServer metrics and etcd metrics around incident
- Node describe outputs for any nodes that drained/NotReady
- CNI pod logs and conntrack counts
- List of pods evicted and restart counts
- Timeline of actions taken by on-call and timestamps

This doc is intended to be kept lightweight and practical. Update owners/timelines after an incident retro.

Revision history:
- 2024-11-07: initial draft (Priya Nair)
- 2024-11-09: added CNI conntrack guidance (Marcus Chen)
- 2025-02-14: added automation action items and escalation path (Lena Ortiz)
